newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwandan refugees flood home, peace force doubts.
newsitem.headline: Rwandan refugees flood home, peace force doubts.

text.p: The return home of half a million Rwandan Hutu refugees has raised doubts among half-hearted members of the multinational peace force for Zaire about the need for military intervention.
The United Nations refugee agency UNHCR estimated on Sunday 400,000 Hutus had already returned to Rwanda from eastern Zaire and that 100,000 more were moving to the border.
"There are 400,000 on this side since this movement started. We could have a total movement of 500,000," UNHCR spokesman Mans Nyberg told a news conference in the Rwandan border town of Gisenyi.
Canada, which is set to lead the multinational force, insisted the mission should go ahead despite the movement of refugees back into Rwanda.
"Now is not the time to pause and reflect. We still have to have very direct action," Canadian Foreign Affairs Minister Lloyd Axworthy told Reuters.

"We're not saying that it will be exactly as we envisioned it two or three days ago because clearly the refugee movement alters that, but it doesn't mean to say that the international presence or involvement no longer is necessary."
Axworthy said large numbers of refugees remained in various parts of eastern Zaire, and their weakened physical condition and other factors might make it difficult for them to join the exodus.
More than a million Hutus fled Rwanda in mid-1994 after a rebel Tutsi army overran the country following the genocide of Tutsis by Hutu extremists. Many ended up in camps in eastern Zaire.

Fearing reprisals if they returned home, and terrified of the armed Hutu militants in their midst, the refugees stayed in their camps until an onslaught this month by Zairean rebels, including many Tutsis, forced the extremists to flee.
Witnesses said the latest arrivals in Gisenyi on Sunday were sicker and weaker than those who started flowing over the border last Friday.

There are still around 215,000 refugees from the area unaccounted for after the fierce fighting of recent weeks, plus some 500,000 other refugees in the Bukavu area of eastern Zaire. Thousands of Zaireans have also been displaced by the fighting.
That leaves big tasks for aid agencies, but countries that were from the start reluctant members of the international peace force have found new reasons to question the need for troops.
They will meet on Wednesday at the U.S. military's European headquarters in Stuttgart, Germany, to review the situation.

U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry stressed on Sunday Washington had yet to make a firm decision on participation. At one point during an NBC television interview, he said: "We are not the Salvation Army."

The Stuttgart meeting was announced at the World Food Summit in Rome by South African Deputy President Thabu Mbeki. Like Washington, South Africa had been a reluctant participant in the force, which was set up to help get food to the refugees.
Some 10,000 soldiers are supposed to join the Canadian-led contingent, but Mbeki said a force that size might not be needed now and the focus would be different anyway.
"I think one of the urgent questions that remains is that you've got these refugees who might have shifted location and are now in Rwanda and who still need to be fed and clothed," he said.
Rwanda has said the force should be scrapped and that the budget for it should be spent on resettling the refugees.

A Canadian advance force was finally allowed out of the airport in Rwanda's capital Kigali on Sunday after being held up for almost a day by bureaucratic foot-dragging by Rwandan authorities, underlining their hostility to the force.
One country that seemed eager to participate in the multinational effort was Burundi.

A senior Burundian official said on Sunday the U.N. special envoy for the Zaire crisis, Raymond Chretien, had approached Burundi's isolated military government about using Bujumbura airport and other facilities to help the intervention force.

Any role in the international effort would lend legitimacy to President Pierre Buyoya's administration and cause consternation among east African states that imposed crippling trade sanctions on Burundi after Buyoya's military coup in July.
